slides.title: Account Tokens
slides.subtitle: Keep a user signed in with a rotating token that never leaves the host
slides.notes: A sign-in returns an Account Token, which is the OAuth refresh token. This example shows how the agent uses it to sign a Session in again, how it rotates, and how it ends. It runs the real AccountTokenClient against Manzanita Outfitters, with real keys over HTTP in one process.

slides.title: Why Account Tokens
slides.statement: Session Tokens are **short-lived**. The Account Token signs the Session in **again**, without asking the user.
slides.notes: Session Tokens expire quickly on purpose. The Account Token lets the agent sign the same Session back in, and it is used only at the company's token and revocation endpoints.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB C["AccountTokenClient"] -- "hold the reference" --> L["pap.accountTokenLock"] C -- "read, replace" --> S[("pap.tokenStore
holds the Account Token")] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB T["Token endpoint
rotates the token"] R["Revocation endpoint
ends the token"] end HOST -- "grant, assertion, DPoP" --> CO HOST -. "status and scopes only" .-> M
slides.caption: The Account Token stays in the host's store; the model learns a status and scope names.
slides.notes: Start inside the host. The AccountTokenClient holds a lock on the token reference, then reads the Account Token from the Reactor token store and later replaces it there. Only the grant, signed with a client assertion and a DPoP proof, crosses to the company, whose token endpoint rotates the token and whose revocation endpoint ends it. Off to the side, the model: it receives only the status and the scope names.

slides.title: A refresh

items.title: Rotate
items.detail: New Session Token and a rotated Account Token

items.title: Replace
items.detail: The new token in the store, before unlocking

slides.notes: The client holds the lock, reads the token, and sends a refresh token grant with the same session_id. The company signs the same Session in again and rotates the token. The new one replaces the old in the store before the lock is released and before the call returns.

slides.title: Two refreshes at once
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Refresh A
  participant B as Refresh B
  participant L as Lock
  participant C as Company
  A->>L: Hold the reference
  B->>L: Hold the reference
  A->>C: Grant with token 1
  C-->>A: Session Token, token 2
  A->>L: Store token 2, release
  B->>C: Grant with token 2
  C-->>B: Session Token, token 3
slides.notes: Two refreshes ask for the same token reference. Refresh A gets the lock first, so B waits for it. Both succeed. A presents token 1, the company rotates it to token 2, and A stores token 2 before releasing the lock. Only then does B go, presenting token 2 rather than the token the company already revoked. Without the lock, both would present token 1 and the second would fail.

slides.title: What the company can answer
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR R["Refresh"] --> Q{"Company answers"} Q -- "rotated" --> S["signed_in
new token stored"] Q -- "invalid_scope" --> C["re_consent_required
ask the user"] Q -- "invalid_grant" --> D["signed_out
token deleted"] V["Revoke"] -- "200" --> X["Every Session signed out
token deleted"]
slides.caption: Wider scopes are a decision for the user, never a retry; expiry and revocation delete the token.
slides.notes: Follow a refresh to the company's answer. Usually the token is rotated, the new one is stored, and the Session is signed in; narrower scopes take this path too. Wider scopes come back as invalid_scope, which the SDK reports as re-consent required: a decision for the user, never a retry. An expired token, 91 days later in the example, draws invalid_grant: the SDK deletes it and the Session carries on signed out. Below, revocation under RFC 7009: once the company answers 200, every Session signed in with that token is signed out and the stored copy is deleted.

slides.title: What stays where
slides.notes: The model learns the status, whether the token rotated, and which scopes it has. Every credential stays in Reactor stores, behind opaque references.

slides.title: In TypeScript
slides.statement: `new AccountTokenClient({ reactor, fetch })`, with `refresh(reference, { context, sessionId, scopes })` and `revoke()`.
slides.notes: TypeScript has the same client, and the lock is contributed at the AccountTokenLocks contribution point.
